self-test · the bridge

The in-page chip runs the SAME runSelfTest() the Node twin runs. One hump, two clocks: the flow's rim eigenvalue is −r (never forks); the map's fixed-point slope is 2−r (forks at exactly r=3). Hover a leg for what it proves.

Both parent cores are imported byte-untouched (the conservatory ODE · the bifurcation map); the FLOW and MAP adapters are code-disjoint, and index.html's CORE region is the byte-twin of core.mjs — re-proven by core.test.mjs.
a cross · the conservatory × the road into chaos

There is exactly one hump here — the parabola r·x(1−x). Hand it to a continuous clock (a flow) and it always glides to one calm level and rests — for every r, forever. Hand the same hump to a discrete clock (one jump per tick) and it splits — past r=3 the level forks in two, then four, then boils into chaos. Same hump. Two clocks. Opposite fates. Drag the brass lever and watch the right dish leave the left behind.

the flow · why it never forks

The continuous clock obeys N′ = r·N(1−N). Its only interior rest is N=1, and its stability is the field's slope there: f′(1) = −r. That is negative for every r>0 — it can never cross zero — so the rest is stable for all r. There is no bifurcation to have. At r=3.9 the left dish still just fills and holds.

the crowd · why it splits

The discrete clock obeys x ← r·x(1−x), one jump per tick. Its fixed point holds only while |f′(x*)| = |2−r| < 1 — so it loses stability at exactly r=3 (|2−3|=1). Past 3 the level rings between two, then four, then — past r≈3.57 — it boils (Lyapunov λ>0). Same hump; tick-by-tick is a different fate.
